intro: Fertőújlak is a village on the Hungarian shore of Lake Fertő, the Neusiedler See, in the Fertő-Hanság national park. At the inn at Mexikópuszta, a stop for walkers and birdwatchers in the marshes, a reader found a tree whose trunk and limbs twist round each other like knotted rope, and sent us its photograph. We do not yet know its species for certain, or its age.
meta_description: A knotted, twisting tree at the Mexikópuszta inn by Fertőújlak on Lake Fertő, Hungary, sent by a reader: where it is and what we know.
question_meta: A knotted, twisting tree at the Mexikópuszta inn by Fertőújlak on Lake Fertő, Hungary, sent by a reader: where it is and what we know.
question_answer: The tree grows in the grounds of the Mexikópusztai Betérő, an inn near Fertőújlak in the Fertő-Hanság national park. Visit when the inn is open.
question_context: A reader stopping at the Mexikópusztai Betérő, an inn on the edge of the Fertő-Hanság marshes near Fertőújlak, looked up and sent us this tree with a GPS fix taken beneath it. Its grey trunk is thick and ridged, and the wood has grown in loops and coils, one limb curling right round another and back again, so that the whole tree looks knotted like an old rope. A dense tangle of thin branches hangs down on every side, carrying small leaflets in rows, which put it in the pea family. The twisting suggests a tree grown for its shape, perhaps a weeping pagoda tree or a contorted locust, but we would rather ask than guess. We do not know its age or who planted it. The inn sits among the reed beds and meadows of the national park on the Hungarian side of Lake Fertő, the lake Austrians call the Neusiedler See. We have not confirmed whether the grounds are open when the inn is closed, so come in its hours and stand right underneath to look up into the knots.

trees.story:
A reader stopping at the inn at Mexikópuszta, on the Hungarian shore of Lake Fertő near Fertőújlak, looked up and found this, and sent us the photograph with a GPS fix taken beneath it.

It is hard to say where the trunk ends and the branches begin. The grey bark is thick and ridged, and the wood under it has grown in loops and coils, one limb curling right round another and back again, so that the whole tree looks knotted, like a rope someone tied and then left for a century. Above the knots a dense tangle of thin branches hangs down on every side, hung with small leaflets in rows.

Those leaflets put it in the pea family, and the twisting suggests a tree grown for its shape, perhaps a weeping pagoda tree or a contorted locust. We would rather not guess which. If you know this tree, or the inn's story of it, tell us here, and tell us its age if anyone there knows it.

Stand right underneath, as the reader did, and look up into the knots.
